cards.title: Three-tier audience taxonomy: TAM, ICP and persona
cards.summary: Separate total addressable market, fit-based ICP and buying-committee personas to plan reach, campaigns and metric vocabulary.
cards.use_when: You or a colleague keep conflating TAM, ICP and persona, or campaign briefs lack a clear audience boundary before content planning.
steps: Define TAM as the broadest layer: everyone who could be interested in the product. Use it for overall business planning and sizing the opportunity.

Narrow to ICP (ideal customer profile), which the source frames mainly for B2B: the target firmographic profile you want to sell into, plus the department-level decision maker. Example: director of marketing at a mid-market manufacturing company in the Northeast.

Narrow further to persona: the individual stakeholder inside that account's buying committee (e.g., director of marketing, head of IT, head of sales). Each has different daily tasks, career goals, pain points and measurement vocabulary.
Size and characterize each layer: note how many people/accounts fall into TAM, ICP and each persona, then use that to prioritize what work you do.
Match message vocabulary to the persona's role: marketers respond to CPL and ROAS; sellers to quota, pipeline and president's club.
Use the three layers to decide campaigns, channels, content topics and the specific individual you are communicating with.
caveats: The source presents the taxonomy as foundational work to do up front, not an ongoing growth motion.
ICP criteria lean B2B/firmographic in this discussion; adapt the layers differently for B2C contexts.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Run five 30-minute qualitative customer interviews
cards.summary: A quick, low-cost interview protocol: pick your top five customers and ask for 30 minutes each to capture language and situation.
cards.use_when: You lack a documented ICP or persona and need raw customer language fast, or want the qualitative layer that surveys and CRM fields cannot provide.
steps: Pick your top five customers.
Ask each if you can spend 30 minutes going through what is going on for them. The source reports customers want to get on the phone and share what they are going through.
On the call, capture the conversation as an auto-generated transcript if the customer is open to being recorded/transcribed.
Keep the format conversational rather than a rigid survey; the goal is unstructured language, not clean responses.
Treat interviews as one of the easier and quicker qualitative starting points, even though the volume of work can sound long and hard before you begin.
caveats: Five interviews is framed as a rapid starting point, not statistical validation.
Get consent before recording or transcribing calls.
The transcript is raw input; it still has to be synthesized before it becomes a usable profile.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Source data externally and pull CRM firmographics
cards.summary: Combine external research (surveys, interviews, social mining) with internal CRM fields to assemble the ICP data picture.
cards.use_when: You are assembling ICP data and trying to work out where the evidence should come from for a specific company size.
steps: Gather external data: customer surveys, direct customer conversations and social platforms such as LinkedIn, Reddit and Instagram where prospects discuss pain points and solution needs.
Improve your collection prompt for communities: ask what pain points people have, or what they would want if you were designing a solution for their industry.
Pull internal data: industry, company size, location, seniority and job profile already in your CRM or database.
Mine sales and support calls for recurring pain points, company types and who on the buying side seeks information.

If you lack a CRM, use LinkedIn to research target accounts in your market, and use sales/call transcripts if you have them; the source jokes you could simply get a CRM, so treat tooling as a sourcing decision, not a blocker.
Package everything together into the data layer you will use to define ICP or persona.
caveats: Which data you can access depends on company size and existing tooling.
No CRM and no transcripts means leaning more heavily on community mining and direct conversations.
The source notes only 48% of over 300 surveyed marketers had a clear, well-documented ICP, so starting from thin data is common.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Synthesize unstructured transcripts into an ICP with an LLM
cards.summary: Feed call transcripts, survey data, CRM firmographics and content performance into an LLM and ask it to define the ICP and surface themes.
cards.use_when: You have raw qualitative data and need to turn it into a tangible ICP or persona document for the team and tools.
steps: Collect the inputs: AI transcripts from the five customer calls, customer survey results and CRM firmographic data.
Include your own content performance data so the model can see what resonates with the audience.

Upload everything into a dedicated project/knowledge base in a tool such as ChatGPT or Claude, which the source treats as context for the LLM. Verify the current interface for creating and sharing a project before instructing a team.
Ask direct questions: who am I speaking to, what are their pain points, what do they care about most, what themes keep recurring.
Ask the model to define an ICP from the supplied demographics and qualitative learning, then turn it into something tangible you can use or share with the team.
Also load information about your own company, products, features and pricing so the model can connect what you offer with what the audience needs.
caveats: This is intended to compress hours or weeks of team synthesis, not to replace the raw data; output quality depends on input quality.
Review the output against source transcripts before treating it as the documented ICP.
Tool project features change; confirm current behavior in the LLM you use.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Use a live LLM persona as an on-demand focus group
cards.summary: Keep the ICP or persona in an interactive LLM project so marketers can test whether copy, campaigns and positioning will resonate before publishing.
cards.use_when: Your persona lives in a PDF nobody opens, or marketers need a fast way to stress-test messaging, positioning and content ideas.
steps: Create a dedicated LLM project containing the persona/ICP knowledge base and use it for every new project rather than sharing a static document.
Have marketers ask the project questions: would this resonate with this ICP, will she hate it, how should I position this, what words should I use.
Treat the answers as a directional check, not binary: ask how to tweak the message to make it as impactful as possible, not only whether it works.
Where your publishing platform supports saving a persona, save it so new content gets automatic QA signals against that ICP. Check your platform's current capabilities.
Use the project as an alignment mechanism for new hires and long-tenured staff, so everyone agrees who we are talking to and what that person cares about.
caveats: The source calls this an on-demand free focus group; it is a messaging QA aid, not a substitute for real customer validation.
Automatic QA checks and persona saving depend on the platform's current features.
The source's working example persona (Growth Gabby) is internally specific and is not a universal template.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Set content altitude by persona seniority
cards.summary: Use the persona to decide whether a topic is covered at the introductory 101 level or the advanced 301 level.
cards.use_when: You are planning content topics and there is disagreement about how deep or advanced the coverage should be.
steps: Work from the persona's experience and daily tasks rather than a generic content calendar.

Example: an experienced marketing leader persona has already set up many Facebook pages and is generating leads and revenue from Meta ads, so they need more advanced content; a 101 piece on setting up a Facebook page answers a question they are not asking.
Call this the altitude decision: 101 versus 301, per topic and per audience.

Do not treat covering multiple audiences or topic levels as a mistake; the source says there is nothing wrong with covering different topics or audiences, but doing the up-front work lets you get specific about which channel and content are for whom.
Feed audience context and your own content-performance data into the LLM task so altitude decisions are grounded in what already resonates.
caveats: The Growth Gabby example is the source's internal persona, not a proven benchmark for other businesses.
The source presents altitude as a persona-driven content planning decision, not a universal rule about always going advanced.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Separate ICP data layer from persona scope: firmographics vs committee roles
cards.summary: Keep firmographic target-account data at the ICP level and role-specific tasks, goals and metric vocabulary at the persona level.
cards.use_when: You are building the ICP record and need to decide which fields belong to the account profile versus each buying-committee member.
steps: For the ICP layer, collect firmographic features: industry, location, company size, seniority and job profile. For example, director of marketing at a manufacturing company in the Northeast.
Identify the decision-making department you want to talk to; for marketing software this is often the director or head of marketing.
For the persona layer, model each individual in the buying committee separately, including roles outside your primary buyer such as head of IT or head of sales.
Capture for each persona: daily tasks, career goals, pain points and the specific vocabulary they use for success.
Use that difference to drive campaigns and content strategy per role rather than one blended message to the whole account.
Size each layer (TAM, ICP, each persona) to prioritize where to spend effort.
caveats: The buying-committee framing is presented as primarily B2B; B2C needs adaptation.
The source positions persona work down here as a growth capability, while the TAM/ICP/persona taxonomy and interview method are baseline.
cards.source_name: How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP).docx

cards.title: Use social communities when CRM and transcripts are missing
cards.summary: Mine Reddit, LinkedIn and Instagram pain-point threads when you have no CRM data or call transcripts to start from.
cards.use_when: You are starting from zero data and cannot yet run customer interviews or pull CRM records.
steps: Search Reddit and similar communities for people asking about pain points in your industry, or prompt the community with what they would want from a solution.
Search LinkedIn for target companies and job profiles in your market to build a picture of the target account set.
Consider Instagram and other social platforms where your audience discusses the problem.
You can also ask an LLM to help you understand market trends and the most common personas or ICP profiles in the space, and adapt the answer to whether it is B2B or B2C.
See this as a temporary data layer, not the destination: the source's recommendation for the highest-quality layer is to get on the phone with someone and capture a transcript.
caveats: Community mining is external, self-selected and lower confidence than direct customer conversations.
LLM answers about market trends are not a substitute for your own customer data.
